claim: Behavioral discrimination threshold gradually decreases during the time course of learning in monkey M1 (n = 31 sessions, p = 1.42 × 10⁻⁵, ANOVA test).
source: Figure 1B shows that, as expected, behavioral discrimination threshold gradually decreases during the time course of learning (monkey M1: n = 31 sessions, p = 1.42 10−5; monkey M2: n = 17 sessions, p = 0.028, ANOVA test; each of blocks 2–4 is characterized by a lower threshold than block 1, p < 0.05, post hoc multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test with specific p-value) of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B, which displays discrimination threshold across blocks.

claim: Behavioral discrimination threshold gradually decreases during the time course of learning in monkey M2 (n = 17 sessions, p = 0.028, ANOVA test).
source: Figure 1B shows that, as expected, behavioral discrimination threshold gradually decreases during the time course of learning (monkey M1: n = 31 sessions, p = 1.42 10−5; monkey M2: n = 17 sessions, p = 0.028, ANOVA test; each of blocks 2–4 is characterized by a lower threshold than block 1, p < 0.05, post hoc multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test with specific p-value) of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Each of blocks 2–4 is characterized by a lower discrimination threshold than block 1 (p < 0.05, post hoc multiple comparisons).
source: Figure 1B shows that, as expected, behavioral discrimination threshold gradually decreases during the time course of learning (monkey M1: n = 31 sessions, p = 1.42 10−5; monkey M2: n = 17 sessions, p = 0.028, ANOVA test; each of blocks 2–4 is characterized by a lower threshold than block 1, p < 0.05, post hoc multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by post hoc statistical comparisons of behavioral data across blocks.

claim: The largest improvement in behavioral performance occurred between blocks 1 and 2, followed by performance saturation after block 2.
source: Interestingly, the largest improvement in behavioral performance occurred between blocks 1 and 2, followed by performance saturation after block 2 (on average, the image orientation discrimination threshold decreased from 18.9o to 4.5o, that is, a 76.2% decrease at the end of the session).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of behavioral threshold changes across blocks, showing a 76.2% decrease.

claim: The image orientation discrimination threshold decreased from 18.9° to 4.5° on average, representing a 76.2% decrease at the end of the session.
source: Interestingly, the largest improvement in behavioral performance occurred between blocks 1 and 2, followed by performance saturation after block 2 (on average, the image orientation discrimination threshold decreased from 18.9o to 4.5o, that is, a 76.2% decrease at the end of the session).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of discrimination threshold at the beginning and end of sessions.

claim: Learning did not significantly influence population mean firing rate during the test stimulus presentation (n = 105 sites, p > 0.9, balanced one-way parametric ANOVA test).
source: Indeed, Figure 1G shows that the population mean firing rate and d' throughout the test stimulus presentation (n = 105 sites) did not differ during the time course of learning (balanced one-way parametric ANOVA test, p > 0.9 for mean firing rate; p > 0.1 for d').
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test) of neuronal firing rate data across learning blocks.

claim: Learning did not significantly influence neuronal discrimination performance (d') during the test stimulus presentation (n = 105 sites, p > 0.1, balanced one-way parametric ANOVA test).
source: Indeed, Figure 1G shows that the population mean firing rate and d' throughout the test stimulus presentation (n = 105 sites) did not differ during the time course of learning (balanced one-way parametric ANOVA test, p > 0.9 for mean firing rate; p > 0.1 for d').
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test) of neuronal discrimination performance across learning blocks.

claim: 15.4% of cells increased their firing rates during learning (p < 0.05, ANOVA test, post hoc comparing blocks 1 and 4).
source: For individual cells, we found that 15.4% cells increased their firing rates, whereas 17.3% showed a decrease (p < 0.05, ANOVA test, post hoc comparing blocks 1 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of individual cell firing rates comparing early and late learning blocks.

claim: 17.3% of cells showed a decrease in firing rates during learning (p < 0.05, ANOVA test, post hoc comparing blocks 1 and 4).
source: For individual cells, we found that 15.4% cells increased their firing rates, whereas 17.3% showed a decrease (p < 0.05, ANOVA test, post hoc comparing blocks 1 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of individual cell firing rates comparing early and late learning blocks.

claim: LFP power did not change significantly across blocks of trials in any frequency band (ANOVA and Kruskal–Wallis tests, p > 0.15).
source: Additionally, we compared LFP power changes relative to block 1 but did not find significant differences across blocks of trials in any frequency band (Figure 1H, ANOVA and Kruskal–Wallis tests, p > 0.15; we also examined the event-related potentials, or ERPs, for the target and test stimuli, but they did not change across blocks; target: p = 0.66, and test: p = 0.59, ANOVA tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests) of LFP power measurements across blocks.

claim: Event-related potentials (ERPs) for the target and test stimuli did not change across blocks (target: p = 0.66, test: p = 0.59, ANOVA tests).
source: Additionally, we compared LFP power changes relative to block 1 but did not find significant differences across blocks of trials in any frequency band (Figure 1H, ANOVA and Kruskal–Wallis tests, p > 0.15; we also examined the event-related potentials, or ERPs, for the target and test stimuli, but they did not change across blocks; target: p = 0.66, and test: p = 0.59, ANOVA tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA tests) of event-related potentials across blocks.

claim: Rapid learning is associated with an increase in low-frequency spike-field coherence (SFC), particularly in the theta band (4–8 Hz), during stimulus presentation intervals.
source: Clearly, rapid learning is associated with an increase in low-frequency SFC (particularly in the theta band, 4–8 Hz) during the intervals when the two stimuli are presented (0–300 ms and 1300–1600 ms. In contrast, SFC at higher frequency bands (alpha, beta, and gamma bands) was either unchanged or slightly decreased during the time course of learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of spike-field coherence data shown in Figure 2A,B, demonstrating increased theta SFC during learning.

claim: SFC at higher frequency bands (alpha, beta, and gamma bands) was either unchanged or slightly decreased during the time course of learning.
source: Clearly, rapid learning is associated with an increase in low-frequency SFC (particularly in the theta band, 4–8 Hz) during the intervals when the two stimuli are presented (0–300 ms and 1300–1600 ms. In contrast, SFC at higher frequency bands (alpha, beta, and gamma bands) was either unchanged or slightly decreased during the time course of learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of spike-field coherence data across different frequency bands during learning.

claim: Learning was associated with an increase in theta SFC during stimulus presentation intervals (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, comparing blocks 2–4 vs block 1 for time intervals 150–270 ms and 1430–1550 ms).
source: These results were confirmed for the population of spike-LFP pairs (Figure 2C)—learning was associated with an increase in theta SFC during the intervals when the two stimuli are presented (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, by comparing theta SFC in blocks 2–4 vs block 1 for time intervals 150–270 ms and 1430–1550 ms; SFC was calculated within a 300-ms window sliding every 10 ms), whereas coherence in the high-frequency bands did not change across blocks of learning (p > 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) of population spike-LFP coherence data during specific time intervals.

claim: Coherence in the high-frequency bands did not change across blocks of learning (p > 0.05).
source: These results were confirmed for the population of spike-LFP pairs (Figure 2C)—learning was associated with an increase in theta SFC during the intervals when the two stimuli are presented (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, by comparing theta SFC in blocks 2–4 vs block 1 for time intervals 150–270 ms and 1430–1550 ms; SFC was calculated within a 300-ms window sliding every 10 ms), whereas coherence in the high-frequency bands did not change across blocks of learning (p > 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike-LFP coherence in high-frequency bands across learning blocks.

claim: SFC in higher frequency bands showed no significant change across blocks (Kruskal–Wallis, p > 0.2).
source: We thus computed the mean SFC values (across all pairs and sessions) and found that whereas SFC in the higher frequency bands showed no significant change across blocks (Kruskal–Wallis, p > 0.2), theta-band SFC was significantly increased during the time course of learning (Figure 3A; n = 625 pairs, comparing blocks 2–4 with block 1, Kruskal–Wallis, p < 10−7).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test) of mean SFC values across frequency bands.

claim: Theta-band SFC was significantly increased during the time course of learning (n = 625 pairs, comparing blocks 2–4 with block 1, Kruskal–Wallis, p < 10⁻⁷).
source: We thus computed the mean SFC values (across all pairs and sessions) and found that whereas SFC in the higher frequency bands showed no significant change across blocks (Kruskal–Wallis, p > 0.2), theta-band SFC was significantly increased during the time course of learning (Figure 3A; n = 625 pairs, comparing blocks 2–4 with block 1, Kruskal–Wallis, p < 10−7).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test) of theta-band SFC across learning blocks with a large sample size.

claim: Learning is accompanied by a pronounced increase in theta SFC in blocks 2–4 relative to block 1 (p < 0.05, t-test).
source: Figure 3B shows the distribution of SFC values for all the pairs in our population and reveals that learning is accompanied by a pronounced increase in theta SFC in blocks 2–4 relative to block 1 (p < 0.05, t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of the distribution of theta SFC values shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Post hoc analysis shows a significant SFC increase in each of blocks 2, 3, and 4 relative to block 1 (p < 0.05).
source: Furthermore, post hoc analysis shows a significant SFC increase in each of blocks 2, 3, and 4 relative to block 1 (p < 0.05; the median theta SFC was increased by 34%).
evidence: The claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis comparing individual blocks to block 1.

claim: The median theta SFC was increased by 34% during learning.
source: Furthermore, post hoc analysis shows a significant SFC increase in each of blocks 2, 3, and 4 relative to block 1 (p < 0.05; the median theta SFC was increased by 34%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of median theta SFC changes during learning.

claim: The increase in theta SFC during learning was statistically significant in both animals (p < 0.001, Kruskal–Wallis test, post hoc analysis).
source: The increase in theta SFC during learning was statistically significant in both animals (Figure 3C, p < 0.001, Kruskal–Wallis test, post hoc analysis).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc analysis) showing consistent effects across both experimental subjects.

claim: The increase in theta SFC during learning was slightly larger when the spike-LFP pairs were taken from different electrodes (n = 523 pairs), but the effects were highly significant in both cases (Kruskal–Wallis test).
source: However, although the increase in theta SFC during learning was slightly larger when the spike-LFP pairs were taken from different electrodes (n = 523 pairs), the effects were highly significant in both cases (Figure 3D, Kruskal–Wallis test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing theta SFC changes for same-electrode vs. different-electrode pairs.

claim: The changes in theta SFC did not depend on the distance between electrode pairs (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 10⁻¹¹ for both 'near' (<2 mm) and 'far' (>2 mm) pairs).
source: Although we divided our SFC pairs into near (<2 mm) and far (>2 mm) groups (345 'near' and 280 'far' pairs), we found that the changes in theta SFC did not depend on the distance between electrode pairs (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 10−11 for both 'near' and 'far' pairs, see Figure 3E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) comparing theta SFC changes for near and far electrode pairs.

claim: There was a gradual increase in theta spike-LFP coherence across trials that matched the time course of the behavioral improvement during learning.
source: As shown in Figure 4, there was a gradual increase in theta spike-LFP coherence across trials that matched the time course of the behavioral improvement during learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of theta SFC and behavioral performance using a sliding window approach shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both the changes in theta spike-LFP coherence and the improvement in discrimination occur gradually during learning.
source: This indicates that both the changes in theta spike-LFP coherence and the improvement in discrimination occur gradually during learning.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the gradual trial-by-trial analysis showing parallel changes in theta SFC and behavioral performance.

claim: The median SFC in block 1 was not significantly different from that in blocks 2–4 in any of the windows of the delay period (p > 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test for each delay interval).
source: However, we found that the median SFC in block 1 was not significantly different from that in blocks 2–4 in any of the windows of the delay period (Figure 5, p > 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test for each delay interval).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) of SFC during the delay period across learning blocks.

claim: The improvement in behavioral performance during learning is unlikely to be explained by a change in the working memory load when novel images are presented during training.
source: This indicates that the improvement in behavioral performance during learning is unlikely to be explained by a change in the working memory load when novel images are presented during training.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of SFC changes during the delay period, which would be expected if working memory load changed.

claim: There was no significant correlation between small changes in firing rate and theta SFC (r = 0.0178, p = 0.5711, Pearson correlation).
source: However, we could not find a significant correlation between these two measures (r = 0.0178, p = 0.5711, Pearson correlation).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between firing rate changes and theta SFC.

claim: Even when comparing z-scored coherence values, theta SFC was still significantly elevated after block 1 (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: We found that even when we compared the z-scored coherence values, theta SFC was still significantly elevated after block 1 (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), whereas the z-score coherence in the other frequency bands either showed no change (in alpha and beta bands, p > 0.1) or decreased only slightly in the gamma band (p < 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) of z-scored coherence values, which control for bias due to firing rates.

claim: The z-score coherence in alpha and beta bands showed no change (p > 0.1).
source: We found that even when we compared the z-scored coherence values, theta SFC was still significantly elevated after block 1 (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), whereas the z-score coherence in the other frequency bands either showed no change (in alpha and beta bands, p > 0.1) or decreased only slightly in the gamma band (p < 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of z-scored coherence values in alpha and beta bands.

claim: The z-score coherence in the gamma band decreased only slightly (p < 0.01).
source: We found that even when we compared the z-scored coherence values, theta SFC was still significantly elevated after block 1 (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), whereas the z-score coherence in the other frequency bands either showed no change (in alpha and beta bands, p > 0.1) or decreased only slightly in the gamma band (p < 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of z-scored coherence values in the gamma band.

claim: Changes in theta SFC induced by learning are unrelated to changes in neuronal firing rates.
source: Altogether, these results further confirm that changes in theta SFC induced by learning are unrelated to changes in neuronal firing rates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple analyses showing theta SFC changes persist after controlling for firing rate effects.

claim: The increase in theta SFC is more prominent in block 2 when learning rate is the highest, followed by a decrease in blocks 3 and 4 when behavioral performance stabilizes (post hoc test, p < 0.05 for block 3 vs 2; p < 0.001 for block 4 vs 3).
source: The analysis in Figure 3 indicates that the increase in theta SFC is more prominent in block 2 when learning rate is the highest, followed by a decrease in blocks 3 and 4 when behavioral performance stabilizes (post hoc test, p < 0.05 for the decrease in theta SFC in block 3 vs 2; p < 0.001 for block 4 vs 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of theta SFC changes across blocks, showing peak increase in block 2.

claim: For familiar image sessions (n = 23), the orientation discrimination threshold was <5° in block 1 and performance did not improve further during the session (p > 0.5 for each block comparison; ANOVA test).
source: Indeed, for familiar image sessions (n = 23), we found that, as expected, the orientation discrimination threshold was <5o in block 1 and performance did not improve further during the session (p > 0.5 for each block comparison; ANOVA test, Figure 6A inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test) of behavioral performance in sessions with familiar images.

claim: Sessions in which familiar images were presented were not associated with significant changes in spike-LFP coherence in any frequency band (p > 0.05, Kruskal–Wallis test, comparing SFC in block 1 vs blocks 2–4; n = 625 pairs).
source: Importantly, in contrast to novel images, the sessions in which we presented familiar images were not associated with significant changes in spike-LFP coherence in any frequency band (Figure 6A; p > 0.05, Kruskal–Wallis test, comparing SFC in block 1 vs blocks 2–4; n = 625 pairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test) of SFC in familiar image sessions.

claim: For 'no learning' control sessions, behavioral discrimination threshold was high at the beginning of the session (in block 1) and did not undergo statistically significant changes in subsequent blocks (p > 0.1, ANOVA test).
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 6A (top), for the 'no learning' control sessions, behavioral discrimination threshold was high at the beginning of the session (in block 1) and did not undergo statistically significant changes in subsequent blocks (p > 0.1, ANOVA test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test) of behavioral performance in control sessions without learning.

claim: In 'no learning' control sessions, SFC did not change across blocks of trials in any frequency band (p > 0.1, Kruskal–Wallis test, comparing SFC in block 1 vs blocks 2–4; n = 96 pairs).
source: Importantly, examining the changes in spike-LFP coherence for the population of 96 pairs, we found that SFC did not change across blocks of trials in any frequency band (p > 0.1, Kruskal–Wallis test, comparing SFC in block 1 vs blocks 2–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test) of SFC in control sessions without learning.

claim: During passive (inattentive) fixation experiments, there were no statistically significant block-by-block changes in SFC in any frequency band (n = 12 sessions, 741 pairs).
source: Similar results (no statistically significant block-by-block changes in SFC in any frequency band, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) were found when natural images were flashed in the neurons' receptive fields during passive (inattentive) fixation experiments (n = 12 sessions, 741 pairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of SFC during passive fixation experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The coordination of spike timing with the local theta LFP activity only occurs when animals improve their performance during learning.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the coordination of spike timing with the local theta LFP activity only occurs when animals improve their performance during learning, and that the increase in theta SFC does not continue with subsequent exposure to familiar stimuli after learning has stabilized, or in conditions in which learning does not take place.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of theta SFC changes across novel, familiar, and no-learning conditions.

claim: The increase in theta SFC does not continue with subsequent exposure to familiar stimuli after learning has stabilized, or in conditions in which learning does not take place.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the coordination of spike timing with the local theta LFP activity only occurs when animals improve their performance during learning, and that the increase in theta SFC does not continue with subsequent exposure to familiar stimuli after learning has stabilized, or in conditions in which learning does not take place.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from familiar image and no-learning control sessions showing no theta SFC changes.

claim: The decrease in behavioral discrimination threshold is significantly correlated with the increase in theta SFC (r = −0.49, Pearson correlation, p < 0.01).
source: We found that the decrease in behavioral discrimination threshold is significantly correlated with the increase in theta SFC (r = −0.49, Pearson correlation, p < 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between behavioral threshold changes and theta SFC changes shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the change in SFC and behavioral performance in the higher frequency bands (alpha: p = 0.42, beta: 0.94, and gamma: 0.17).
source: In contrast, despite slightly negative trends, there was no significant correlation between the change in SFC and behavioral performance in the higher frequency bands (alpha: p = 0.42, beta: 0.94, and gamma: 0.17; Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between behavioral performance and SFC in different frequency bands.

claim: The increase in behavioral discrimination performance during learning is associated with a tight coordination of spike timing with the local population activity.
source: We have demonstrated that the increase in behavioral discrimination performance during learning is associated with a tight coordination of spike timing with the local population activity.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding supported by multiple analyses of spike-LFP coherence and behavioral performance.

claim: The spike-LFP synchronization associated with learning occurred in the theta band, while higher frequency synchronization was uncorrelated with changes in behavioral performance.
source: The spike-LFP synchronization associated with learning occurred in the theta band, while higher frequency synchronization was uncorrelated with changes in behavioral performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency-specific analysis of SFC changes and their correlation with behavioral performance.

claim: The changes in spike-LFP theta synchronization only characterized the learning of novel stimuli but were absent once stimuli became familiar or in situations when learning did not occur.
source: Importantly, the changes in spike-LFP theta synchronization only characterized the learning of novel stimuli but were absent once stimuli became familiar or in situations when learning did not occur.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of theta SFC changes across novel, familiar, and no-learning conditions.

claim: Plasticity in visual cortex during the time course of learning is accompanied by elevated low-frequency synchronization between individual neuron responses and local population activity.
source: These findings indicate that plasticity in visual cortex during the time course of learning is accompanied by elevated low-frequency synchronization between individual neuron responses and local population activity.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main conclusion based on the observed theta SFC changes during learning.

claim: There was a significant increase in spike-LFP phase locking strength in the theta band during learning despite the fact that theta LFP power remained constant.
source: Additionally, there was a significant increase in spike-LFP phase locking strength in the theta band during learning despite the fact that theta LFP power remained constant.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis showing increased theta SFC without corresponding changes in theta LFP power.

claim: It is possible that the improvement in behavioral performance occurring over larger time scales (e.g., weeks) may be accompanied by similar changes in spike-LFP theta synchronization.
source: Although our study reports neuronal changes associated with a rapid form of learning, it is possible that the improvement in behavioral performance occurring over larger time scales (e.g., weeks) may be accompanied by similar changes in spike-LFP theta synchronization.
evidence: The claim is speculative, extending the findings to longer timescales of learning.

claim: Neuronal oscillations in the theta frequency range (3–8 Hz) have been associated with the induction of synaptic plasticity (Buzsaki, 2002).
source: In particular, neuronal oscillations in the theta frequency range (3–8 Hz) have been associated with the induction of synaptic plasticity (Buzsaki, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Buzsaki (2002).

claim: The timing between incoming stimuli and ongoing theta oscillations controls synaptic changes.
source: For instance, the timing between incoming stimuli and ongoing theta oscillations controls synaptic changes.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about theta oscillations and synaptic plasticity.

claim: Oscillations in the theta range can be modulated by behavior and brain state (Winson, 1978; Hasselmo et al., 2002).
source: In addition, oscillations in the theta range can be modulated by behavior and brain state (Winson, 1978; Hasselmo et al., 2002) and have been assigned a key role in the maintenance of information in short-term memory (Lee et al., 2005; Liebe et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Winson (1978) and Hasselmo et al. (2002).

claim: Theta oscillations have been assigned a key role in the maintenance of information in short-term memory (Lee et al., 2005; Liebe et al., 2012).
source: In addition, oscillations in the theta range can be modulated by behavior and brain state (Winson, 1978; Hasselmo et al., 2002) and have been assigned a key role in the maintenance of information in short-term memory (Lee et al., 2005; Liebe et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Lee et al. (2005) and Liebe et al. (2012).

claim: Animals that exhibit more theta activity show elevated classical conditioning of the nictitating membrane response in rabbit hippocampus (Berry and Thompson, 1978).
source: Our results are consistent with previous evidence in rabbit hippocampus (Berry and Thompson, 1978) that animals that exhibit more theta activity show elevated classical conditioning of the nictitating membrane response.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Berry and Thompson (1978).

claim: Attention and alertness have been previously associated with elevated neuronal firing in area V4 (Fries et al., 1997; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Fries et al., 2001).
source: Indeed, although attention and alertness have been previously associated with elevated neuronal firing in area V4 (Fries et al., 1997; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Fries et al., 2001), increased neuronal sensitivity (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999), increased gamma LFP power (Fries et al., 1997, 2001), and increased gamma spike-LFP synchrony (Fries et al., 1997; Jarvis and Mitra, 2001), none of these measures changed significantly across blocks of trials (p > 0.1, for both animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Fries et al. (1997), McAdams and Maunsell (1999), and Fries et al. (2001).

claim: Attention and alertness have been associated with increased neuronal sensitivity (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999).
source: Indeed, although attention and alertness have been previously associated with elevated neuronal firing in area V4 (Fries et al., 1997; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Fries et al., 2001), increased neuronal sensitivity (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999), increased gamma LFP power (Fries et al., 1997, 2001), and increased gamma spike-LFP synchrony (Fries et al., 1997; Jarvis and Mitra, 2001), none of these measures changed significantly across blocks of trials (p > 0.1, for both animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by McAdams and Maunsell (1999).

claim: Attention and alertness have been associated with increased gamma LFP power (Fries et al., 1997, 2001).
source: Indeed, although attention and alertness have been previously associated with elevated neuronal firing in area V4 (Fries et al., 1997; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Fries et al., 2001), increased neuronal sensitivity (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999), increased gamma LFP power (Fries et al., 1997, 2001), and increased gamma spike-LFP synchrony (Fries et al., 1997; Jarvis and Mitra, 2001), none of these measures changed significantly across blocks of trials (p > 0.1, for both animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Fries et al. (1997, 2001).

claim: Attention and alertness have been associated with increased gamma spike-LFP synchrony (Fries et al., 1997; Jarvis and Mitra, 2001).
source: Indeed, although attention and alertness have been previously associated with elevated neuronal firing in area V4 (Fries et al., 1997; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Fries et al., 2001), increased neuronal sensitivity (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999), increased gamma LFP power (Fries et al., 1997, 2001), and increased gamma spike-LFP synchrony (Fries et al., 1997; Jarvis and Mitra, 2001), none of these measures changed significantly across blocks of trials (p > 0.1, for both animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Fries et al. (1997) and Jarvis and Mitra (2001).

claim: None of the attention/alertness-related measures (firing rate, sensitivity, gamma LFP power, gamma spike-LFP synchrony) changed significantly across blocks of trials (p > 0.1, for both animals).
source: Indeed, although attention and alertness have been previously associated with elevated neuronal firing in area V4 (Fries et al., 1997; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Fries et al., 2001), increased neuronal sensitivity (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999), increased gamma LFP power (Fries et al., 1997, 2001), and increased gamma spike-LFP synchrony (Fries et al., 1997; Jarvis and Mitra, 2001), none of these measures changed significantly across blocks of trials (p > 0.1, for both animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant changes in attention-related measures during learning.

claim: There was no significant relationship between the horizontal/vertical saccade amplitude and frequency and block number (p > 0.4, Pearson correlation for each comparison).
source: We also failed to find changes in eye movements during learning—there was no significant relationship between the horizontal/vertical saccade amplitude and frequency and block number (p > 0.4, Pearson correlation for each comparison).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of eye movement parameters across learning blocks.

claim: The increase in theta coherence during learning is unlikely to have been contaminated by gradual changes in behavioral context or fixational eye movements during the time course of the session.
source: This indicates that the increase in theta coherence during learning is unlikely to have been contaminated by gradual changes in behavioral context or fixational eye movements during the time course of the session.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of changes in attention-related measures and eye movements during learning.

claim: Performance in the match trials (bar release responses) did not significantly deteriorate across blocks of trials (p > 0.1; ANOVA test).
source: However, we did not find statistically significant changes in match (bar release) responses across blocks of trials (by analyzing all the sessions with an improvement in learning performance, p > 0.1; ANOVA test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test) of match trial performance across blocks.

claim: After 150 trials of passive (unattended) exposure to the image followed by the image discrimination task, a gradual improvement in discrimination threshold was found (p < 0.01, ANOVA test; each of blocks 2–4 was characterized by a lower threshold than block 1, p < 0.05, post hoc multiple comparisons).
source: As expected, as the monkey did not actually practice the image orientation discrimination task for the stimuli he was exposed to, we found a gradual improvement in behavioral discrimination threshold during the session (p < 0.01, ANOVA test; each of blocks 2–4 was characterized by a lower threshold than block 1, p < 0.05, post hoc multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test with post hoc comparisons) of behavioral data from passive exposure control experiments.

claim: Theta oscillations in areas outside V4 may modulate excitability in areas projecting to and receiving information from V4.
source: Indeed, it is possible that theta oscillations in areas outside V4 may modulate excitability in areas projecting to and receiving information from V4.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for the observed theta synchronization.
